original_question: Let (Omega, mu) be a sigma-finite measure space, let V be a dense subspace of L2(Omega), let a: V x V -> C be a closed sectorial sesquilinear form, let -A generate the associated bounded analytic semigroup (T(t)) on L2(Omega), and suppose there exists a function g in L-infinity(Omega) with g > 0 mu-almost everywhere and 1/g in L-infinity(Omega) such that ||g T(t)f||_infinity <= ||g f||_infinity for all f in L2(Omega) intersect L-infinity(Omega) and all t >= 0. How can one find or explicitly construct such a weight g?
target_in_paper: Section 6, Problem 24 (Weight construction for L∞-contraction), together with the setup from Problem 21 and the nearby interpretation in Problem 23.
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper’s actual target. It uses the exact form-generated analytic-semigroup framework imported from Problem 21, assumes the existence of a weight g with g > 0 almost everywhere and g^{-1} in L∞(Ω), encodes the paper’s condition (3) by the weighted contractivity inequality ||gT(t)f||∞ ≤ ||gf||∞ for all t ≥ 0 and f in L²(Ω) ∩ L∞(Ω), and asks how such a weight can be found or constructed. That matches Problem 24, not the neighboring existence question in Problem 22 or the characterization question in Problem 23.
missing_details: The paper explicitly works with complex-valued L²(Ω).
It fixes the sesquilinear convention: a is linear in the first argument and antilinear in the second.
A fully stand-alone formulation should say that A is the operator associated with the form a on L²(Ω), since Problem 24 is posed by reference to the full setting of Problem 21.

The nearby context in Problem 23 explains that the issue is whether T can be made contractive on the L∞-closure of V for the equivalent norm f ↦ ||gf||∞; that interpretation is implicit in your draft but not stated.
Positivity of the semigroup and finiteness of μ(Ω) are not assumptions of Problem 24 itself; they appear only in the comments as a possibly useful special case.

In that positive finite-measure special case, the paper gives an equivalent reformulation through the adjoint inequality T(t)^*g ≤ g almost everywhere for all t ≥ 0; this is paper-faithful context that your draft does not mention.
The paper asks how to find or construct such a function g; adding the word explicitly is slightly stronger than the paper’s official phrasing.
refined_question: Let (Ω, μ) be a σ-finite measure space, let V be a dense subspace of the complex space L²(Ω), and let a: V × V → ℂ be a closed sectorial sesquilinear form, linear in the first argument and antilinear in the second. Let A be the operator associated with a on L²(Ω), so that -A generates the corresponding bounded analytic semigroup T = (T(t))_{t ≥ 0}. Assume that there exists a function g in L∞(Ω) with g > 0 μ-almost everywhere and g^{-1} in L∞(Ω) such that ||gT(t)f||L∞ ≤ ||gf||L∞ for every t ≥ 0 and every f in L²(Ω) ∩ L∞(Ω). In this setting, how can one find or construct such a weight g?
equivalent_formulation: Under the additional assumptions stated in the comments to Problem 24 that T is positive and μ(Ω) < ∞, the paper says that condition ||gT(t)f||∞ ≤ ||gf||∞ is equivalent to T(t)^*g ≤ g almost everywhere on Ω for all t ≥ 0. In that special case, Problem 24 can be reformulated as: construct a function g in L∞(Ω) with g > 0 almost everywhere and g^{-1} in L∞(Ω) such that T(t)^*g ≤ g almost everywhere for every t ≥ 0.
justification: The draft targets Problem 24 because it already assumes that a weight satisfying condition (3) exists and asks how to obtain it. If the draft were aiming at Problem 22, it would ask whether such a weight exists at all; if it were aiming at Problem 23, it would ask for a characterization of all semigroups admitting such a weight. Problem 21 supplies the full ambient hypotheses on (Ω, μ), V, a, A, and T, while Problem 23 explains the equivalent-norm viewpoint, and the comments to Problem 24 provide the paper’s own suggested positive finite-measure reformulation via T(t)^*g ≤ g and explain why naive choices such as positive eigenfunctions are not sufficient in general.
